You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:

 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",

     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",

     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{out,avg} \ge 4.5 \text{ V}$
        *   $V_{max} \le 5.5 \text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{ s}$ (startup)
        *   $dV \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 MOhm.
    *   Operating Conditions (S1-S6): Varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, and $R_L$.

    *   `p_sshi_full_bridge` (c0001): High power (passed $V_{out,min}$), but $V_{max}$ way too high (S1: 111V, S3: 23kV - probably simulation instability, but clearly too high). It lacked voltage regulation.
    *   `p_sshi_half_bridge` (c0028): Vout went negative. This usually happens when the biasing/rectification is wrong or the sync pulses are misaligned.
    *   `p_sshi_full_bridge_pos` (c0035): $V_{out}$ too low (~1V). It only used positive edges, reducing power by half.

    *   The `p_sshi_full_bridge` had plenty of power but blew past the $V_{max}$ limit.
    *   A Zener clamp (DZ33) is available, but it clamps at 3.3V, which is below the required 4.5V.
    *   We need a way to regulate the output between 4.5V and 5.5V.
    *   The current structure is a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI).
    *   To limit $V_{out}$, we can:
        1.  Use a Zener-based regulator (not possible with DZ33 since it's 3.3V).
        2.  Use a shunt regulator.
        3.  Control the sync pulses based on $V_{out}$ (but the SYNC controller provided is "ideal" and doesn't have feedback).
        4.  Add a limiting circuit or a more complex rectifier.

    *Wait*, look at the `p_sshi_full_bridge` results again. $V_{out}$ went to 10V, 20V, etc. We need it to stop at 5V. Since we don't have a programmable regulator, we need a passive or semi-passive way to clamp it or a way to reduce the energy transfer once it reaches 5V.

    However, the SYNC controller is just a timer. It doesn't know about $V_{out}$.
    But wait, I have `DZ33` Zeners. If I put two DZ33s in series? No, that's not how it works.
    Wait, if I use a Zener as a voltage reference for a switch? No, the switches are controlled by SYNC.

    Let's reconsider the `p_sshi_full_bridge`. It's effectively a full-bridge rectifier with an inductor-switch (SSHI) to flip the voltage.
    The issue is $V_{max}$ and ripple.

    *   Standard SSHI improves efficiency by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
    *   Full-bridge SSHI:
        $L$ and $S$ are used to flip $V_{C_p}$.
        Rectifier (4 diodes) converts the resulting AC to DC.
        $C_{out}$ smooths it.
    *   The `p_sshi_full_bridge` topology:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn
        This flips the voltage across $C_p$ when $S1$ closes.

    The `p_sshi_full_bridge` had too much power. We need to limit it.
    Could we use a Zener to bleed off excess current? A DZ33 on "out" would clamp to 3.3V (too low).
    What if we use a Zener to prevent the output from rising too high?
    If we use a Zener in the *feedback* path? (No feedback).

    Wait, is there another way to limit $V_{out}$?
    If the output voltage $V_{out}$ is high, the diodes $D1, D2$ only conduct when $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_d$.
    As $V_{out}$ increases, the conduction angle decreases, naturally limiting the power.
    But the SSHI mechanism increases the voltage amplitude significantly, which is why it's overshooting.

    *   $V_{out,min} = 4.5 \text{ V}$
    *   $V_{out,max} = 5.5 \text{ V}$
    *   S3 is the "strong excitation, light load" case ($I_p = 120 \text{ uA}, R_L = 10 \text{ kOhm}$). This is where $V_{out}$ will soar.
    *   S4 is the "weak excitation" case ($I_p = 40 \text{ uA}, R_L = 4.7 \text{ kOhm}$). This is where it might fail $V_{out,min}$.

    If $V_{out}$ is too high in S3, we need more load or a clamp.
    If $V_{out}$ is too low in S4, we need more efficiency.

    The current `p_sshi_full_bridge` has:
    - D1: pzp -> out
    - D2: pzn -> out
    - D3: 0 -> pzp
    - D4: 0 -> pzn
    - L1, S1 for flipping.

    Is there a way to use the SYNC controller to reduce power?
    We could use `edges: pos` instead of `both`. `p_sshi_full_bridge_pos` tried this and it was too weak.

    What if we use a different rectifier? A half-bridge?
    `p_sshi_half_bridge` (c0028) went negative. Let's see why.
    D1: pzp -> out
    C_bias: pzn -> 0
    L1, S1: flipping.
    The bias capacitor $C_{bias}$ is supposed to keep the piezo centered around some voltage. If $C_{bias}$ is too small or the charging is unbalanced, the output can drift.

    Wait, the `p_sshi_half_bridge` output was negative. That means $V(out)$ was pulled down.
    Looking at the components:
    D1: pzp -> out
    C_bias: pzn -> 0
    L1: pzp -> n1
    S1: n1 -> pzn
    When $S1$ closes, it connects pzp and pzn through $L1$.
    If pzp is positive and pzn is 0, current flows $pzp \to L1 \to pzn$.
    This should flip the voltage.
    But there's no way to charge the output capacitor $C1$ other than through $D1$.
    If $D1$ is $pzp \to out$, then $V_{out}$ can only be positive.
    Why did it go negative?
    Ah, $C1$ is $out \to 0$.
    Wait, the results say $vavg = -0.913$ V. This is very strange. $V(out)$ cannot be negative if the only path to it is a diode from $pzp$ and a capacitor to ground.
    Unless... the $1 \text{ GOhm}$ resistor to ground? No.
    Wait, did I misread the `p_sshi_half_bridge` components?
    D1: pzp out
    C_bias: pzn 0
    L1: pzp n1
    S1: n1 pzn
    G1: ton, phase, both
    C1: out 0
    Everything seems correct. Maybe the simulation had a glitch or the `pzn` node was being driven negative?
    The piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ MOhm}$.
    Between $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    If $pzn$ is connected to $C_{bias}$, it's not grounded.

    Let's try a standard SSHI with a more robust rectifier.
    What if we use a full-bridge but with a way to clamp the voltage?
    Since DZ33 is 3.3V, it's not useful for 4.5V.
    What if we use a different topology?
    A "voltage doubler" or "charge pump" might be too much.
